items.title: Examples of conservation of angular momentum

source_refs.note: Examples of conservation of angular momentum: a main subheading of 3.6 Law of conservation of angular momentum, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 68-71.

blocks.text: A man diving from a diving board

A diver jumping from a springboard has to take a few somersaults in air before touching the water surface, as shown in Fig.3.18. After leaving the springboard, he curls his body by rolling arms and legs in. Due to this, his moment of inertia decreases, and he spins in midair with a large angular velocity. When he is about to touch the water surface, he stretches out his arms and legs. He enters the water at a gentle speed and gets a smooth dive. This is an example of the law of conservation of angular momentum.

blocks.alt: A sequence of positions of one diver: walking along the board, raising a knee, taking off stretched out with the arms up, then curled up in three somersault positions with gold arrows showing the spin, and finally stretched out head first for the entry into the water.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.18: A man diving from a diving board (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.18).
blocks.long_description: The book prints this figure as a photo-sequence; it is redrawn here as a sketch.

blocks.text: An ice skater as shown in Fig.3.19 can increase his angular velocity by folding arms and bringing the stretched leg close to the other leg. By doing so, he decreases his moment of inertia. As a result, angular speed increases. When he stretches his hands and a leg outward, the moment of inertia increases and hence angular velocity decreases.

blocks.alt: Two front views of a skater. Left, labelled I - large, ω - small: arms stretched out sideways, with a wide red ring round the arms and a small one round the feet. Right, labelled I - small, ω - large: arms folded across the chest and legs together, with small red rings round the body from chest to feet. Below: Angular momentum = (Moment of inertia) (Angular velocity), L = I x ω.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.19: An ice skater using angular momentum (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.19).

blocks.text: A person holding some weight in his hands standing on a turntable.

A person is standing on a turntable with heavy mass (dumb-bell) in his hands stretched out on both sides as shown in Fig. 3.20. As he draws his hands inward, his angular speed at once increases. This is because the moment of inertia decreases on drawing the hands inwards, which increases the angular speed.

It has been noticed that when ice on the polar caps of Earth melts and water flows away in the form of river; the moment of inertia of water and hence that of Earth about its axis of rotation increases due to conservation of angular momentum. Hence, the angular velocity of Earth will decrease, therefore, the duration of day increases.

blocks.alt: Two sketches of a man standing on a turntable with a dumb-bell in each hand. (a) Arms stretched out sideways, with a dashed circle round the path of the hands. (b) Arms drawn in, the dumb-bells close to his sides. A small curled arrow above each head shows the rotation.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.20: Man with masses in his hands on a turntable; conservation of angular momentum requires that as the man pulls his arms in, the angular velocity increases (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.20).

blocks.text: Flywheel is a mechanical device which consists of a heavy wheel with an axle (Fig. 3.21). It is used to store rotational energy, smooth out output fluctuations and provides stability in a wide range of applications such as bicycles and other vehicles, industrial machinery, gyroscopes, ships and spacecrafts.
The flywheel called the balance wheel regulates the time keeping mechanism in mechanical clocks and watches by maintaining controlled oscillations rate.

blocks.caption: Figure 3.21: A flywheel (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.21).

blocks.text: When a fly wheel spins, its angular momentum resists changes to its orientations, maintaining stability. This is useful in systems that need precise control over their orientation without external interference.

blocks.text: A gyroscope is a device which is used to maintain its orientation relative to the Earth's axis or resists changes in its orientation. It consists of a mounted flywheel pivoted in supporting rings as shown in Fig. 3.22. It works on the basis of law of conservation of angular momentum due to its large moment of inertia. When the gyroscope spins at a large angular speed, it gains large angular momentum. It is then difficult to change the orientation of the gyroscope's rotational axis due to its large moment of inertia. A change in orientation requires a change in its angular momentum. To change the direction of a large angular momentum, a corresponding large torque is required. Even if gyroscope is tilted (Fig. 3.23), it still keeps levitated without falling. Hence, it is a reason why a gyroscope can be used to maintain orientation. The main applications of gyroscope are in the guiding system of aeroplanes, submarines and space vehicles in order to maintain a specific direction in space to keep steady course.

blocks.alt: A gyroscope on a stand: a heavy rotor on a horizontal axle, mounted in an inner ring, a horizontal ring and an outer ring held by the stand. A red arrow along the axle to the left is labelled L = I ω and Angular momentum. On the right a curled arrow round the axle end is labelled Spin axis.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.22: The gyroscope (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.22).

blocks.alt: A toy gyroscope with a dark spinning rotor inside two crossed metal rings. The whole gyroscope is tilted steeply, with only the lower end of its axle resting on the tip of a small round stand, yet it does not fall.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.23: A tilted gyroscope (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.23).

blocks.text: Planets move around the Sun in elliptical orbits with Sun situated at one of its foci, thus, distance of a planet from the Sun is not constant when it is nearer the Sun. Its orbital velocity increases automatically. Why?
